This is, simply put, my favourite game. 

There's nothing quite like Hunt out there. 
It's a difficult, challenging PvPvE game. You play as a bounty hunter tasked with killing a high value target in an area infested with some sort of dark magic. The only problem is, you're not the only hunter out there. 

You collect clues to locate the target, you kill the target, you banish the target.... then you have to escape the map with tokens proving it's you who killed it. 
Maps can hold 12 players, which means there will be 10 more people who are intent on stopping you leaving with that bounty. And almost everything you do can be heard by everyone else on the map, meaning you have to move as quickly as you can, whilst going as quietly as necessary. 

The gameplay loop is incredibly satisfying, with the right balance of risk and reward. Most things you do in a match earn you an amount of cash to take to the next lobby, where you can then either save for a rainy day, or buy higher tier equipment for your next loadout. But, anything you die with is lost to the bayou - hence the risk. If your hunter survives, they get experience and you can use that to buy some traits that make them marginally better for the next run out. 

This system sounds like a "win more" system, where success leads to a higher probability of success on the next run, and so it seems inevitable that the good get better equipment to be even more effective - so how can a new player break in?
The answer is quite simple; all equipment has a situation where it's the best choice. The starting rifle has a larger magazine than most other guns in the game and shoots more quickly, so favours closer quarters fighting. The starting shotgun has the longest one-hit-kill range of all the shotguns. Ultimately, playing to your loadout's strengths and being better than your opponent has a FAR higher contribution to your success than the exact equipment everyone loaded in with.

The barrier to a new player is therefore not an insurmountable equipment difference, it's learning the game. There are (currently) three VERY full maps, each of which is absolutely crammed with minutiae. It's about knowing how to move around compounds without triggering sound traps quickly. It's about knowing which directions you're actually vulnerable from. It's about knowing which sort of gun can shoot through that wooden wall you know they're crouched behind. It's about knowing that when the shot sounds like THAT, that means it's this specific gun and how far away they are. The burden of knowledge you have to accumulate to become proficient is very high. 

It's this burden of knowledge which is the thing you, as a potential buyer, have to consider. 
Are you prepared to get shot from places you don't understand for 20 hours? Are you prepared to be surprised by what their equipment did? You will likely die a lot before you get good. 

But when you DO become proficient, there is nothing like this game. 
Nothing replicates the thrill of you and a partner (or two) methodically outmanoeuvring another team and taking them down. 

Another (major) point in the "pro" column is the developer team. They are extremely active with the community, and listen to and implement suggestions from the community very proactively. They are continually improving the game and adding loads of content. I have bought a lot of the (cosmetic) DLC, purely to support the team, as I have gotten way more out of the game than the price I paid to get in.

Despite every other shooter I try, I keep coming back to Hunt. As long as there are other hunters to go up against, I think I might never stop.

This is an OLD REVIEW that has been updated to the full release version of Hunt: Showdown. Many things have changed, and the review is horribly outdated, so I have done my best to include all of the new updates in the review.


[b] PROS: [/b]


- The atmosphere of the game is amazing. You can really get immersed in the world alone, depsite the lack of NPCs or voice acting.

- Graphics to this game look fantastic, even on low settings.

- Weapons feel good, shoot good, and make you feel powerful with each shot. Also includes bullet speed, and one-shot headshots up to reasonable distances depending on ammo type.

- A leveling system, complete with weapons, perks, abilities, and consumables to unlock and equip, and a near-endless variety to pair and test out together.

- Lots of weapon and character variety. From rifles with bayonets to silenced revolvers. From a noob cowboy with plain pants and a shirt, to legends wearing black dusters covered in skulls, trinkets, and scars.

- Enemy AI variety is good, making you adapt to their fighting styles and how to counter them effectively. Some enemies rush you mindlessly, but others will sit back and try to take you out at a distance. The AI is simple, but effective at their job.

- The sound design. From the crunching of glass under your feet, to crows taking off when people are too close. The way the barn creaks when you take a step. The distant gunshots and being able estimate how far they are by the sound. Everything revolves around sound, and the sound is beautiful.

- Weapon balancing. Every weapon this game is viable. The later weapons may be more powerful, sure, but you have a reduced ammo pool and ammo replenishment compared to earlier weapons, longer reload times, longer pauses in between shots, and a higher price point. You want to be able to keep an enemy suppressed for days? There's a weapon for that. you want to stay calm, and pick them off with a single, well-placed headshot? There's a weapon for that. You want a single-action revolver with a stock and a short range scope? There's a weapon for that... for some reason.
- Random gameplay. Not in the bad way, either. One game you might not hear a peep the entire round, but the next, gunshots are ringing out from every single direction. You never truly know what's going to happen when you drop into the bayou.
- Having an objective. Oh my god, having an objective. It's what separates this game from PUBG and Escape from Tarkov. Having that tangible, ever-present quest in-game, that requires multiple steps to complete most times, makes the game into more than a PvP experience. It's not something that you can be sneaky about most of the time. You have to reveal to EVERYONE where you are to complete your objective.

[b] MEH: [/b]

- The price. This comes down to personal preference, and whether or not you like the amount of content so far. 2 different levels with multiple areas to explore, different times of day, 3 unique bosses, and a metric ton of challenges and weapons to unlock through gameplay.
- The coop. While it is insanely fun, it can be a real pain if you join with a random partner over and over. There is also the choice of playing with group of 3 rather than 2, but can be opted out of if you would just like to play in a duo. This depends on whether or not you have someone to play the game with, and I would highly recommend picking it up if you have a confirmed partner to play with.
- The bosses. The bosses themselves are great, but the variety isn't, with only 3 bosses to go after. This depends on whether you really care about the boss fights, or whether it's the PvP and world that interests you.
- As far as I can tell, you need a beast of a rig to run this thing properly. It doesn't mean that you won't be able to play, but you'll be confined to playing on lower settings. Not a huge loss overall, but some people are all about dem gwaffics and framerates. The game seems to be getting more and more optimised with each update, so it'll hopefully only get better from here.
- The community. I'll go into detail on this later in it's own section, because it's a tough one to cover in a few sentences.


[b] CONS: [/b]


- The loading. Loading screens are long, which is understandable, since the map is massive. The in-game loading of objects and enemies, isn't. Having a hotspot be completely void of life, then spawn in 3 tough AI enemies 30 feet away both ruins the immersion and your planning from time to time.
- The solo play. While you are dropped in without a partner, other people can still join with a partner, putting you at an obvious disadvantage, making solo play quite difficult. You do get a bonus for doing this, but it normally won't apply to you, since you'll end up dead. Not impossible to do, but takes a lot more skill with a meagre offering to balance it out.
- The updates. Every update normally causes some type of havoc, whether it be textures getting broken, rewards not loading properly, or server disconnects. Every update seems to play around with something unintentional, which is probably thanks to the spaghetti code that's held together with masking tape and wrapping paper. Expect a few... weird... occurrences to pop up from time to time.
- The learning curve. If you don't have an experienced teammate to play with, there is a lot of trial-and-error you will be doing, and you will be stomped into the mud. Over and over. I would definitely suggest watching tutorials or videos on youtube on how to actually play, because there are quite a few concepts that aren't explained anywhere in-game. When should you shoot AI? How does poison work exactly? Why did someone throw a lantern at my "dead" friend? This isn't Call of Duty. You won't know everything, and it will be the death of you. Shrug it off, grit your teeth, and jump back in for revenge.


[b] COMMUNITY [/b]

This community should [i]*really*[/i] be avoided for the first little while. While they can be helpful, a large amount have found the mentality of "This game has been ruined by those filthy [i]casual[/i] gamers" due to new updates from the devs. It hasn't really been "casualized", but has been made different from what it once was. Balancing is a fickle thing, and some people would still rather have the game be reverted back to the 0.6 update, or even the 0.1 alpha.

Every single corner of the reddit, steam forums, or elsewhere, are going to be coated in people complaining about how base mechanics and weapons are overpowered, while others claim that they're underpowered. Burning a downed hunter (which slowly removes him from the match unless his teammate revives him in time) is vilified by a lot of people in this game. They cite it as an unfair and stupid tactic, labelling the people who do this "insta-burners". Then you have the crowd who oppose this idea, saying "Is there any reason to not give yourself an obvious advantage over your opponent?".

There's also a lot of hate surrounding the "camping" in this game. This game with have hectic, tense moments, where you run and gun your way through the woods to extraction. But... you'll also have times where the gameplay slows to a crawl, because 2 teams refuse to move. The team inside the house knows that, with their shotguns, they'll be at a disadvantage if they leave their cover to take on the rifle users outside, and the team outside realises the opposite. Therefore, both teams sit on their hands for ~30 minutes without doing anything. This gameplay scenario is looked down upon from every angle, but it's because people want the other group to make a mistake. Both teams are technically making the right decision. you decide on how you want to play, not the community.

[b] VERDICT: [/b]


Overall, despite its flaws,the game is surprisingly stable, and surprisingly fun, for those who can run it. I would suggest picking it up, but I would also suggest picking it up with a friend, or be prepared to get destroyed your first few games.

The 1800s firearms are just super duper well done. Reloading animations take forever (as they should with these guns), in a far more realistic way than most FPS games. When I press the button to reload my revolver, the animation is: I hold the gun up, open the loading port, eject the spent casing, load in a fresh bullet, revolve the cylinder and repeat until fully loaded, close the loading port, spin the cylinder, and pull the hammer back. Story Challenges, as the name suggests, are sets of challenges you can finish for some rewards with some story. [h3]Original review on 26th December, 2024[/h3]

I never thought I will be writing a "Not Recommended" review for this game.

As you can see from my playtime, I've poured quite a huge part of my free time into Hunt. That itself proves my fondness to this game.
I started playing right after its early access, back when there was no "1896" in its title. I was drawn into the grim, ruthless nature of the Hunt; everything around you can and will kill you, and you have to make the most of what you have―your equipment, your trait, your position and your knowledge of other enemies' equipment, trait and position. Forming a strategy is a must to at least survive, even though that means you're leaving without bounty. You need to traverse the map carefully, paying attention to the surroundings, and plan your next move deliberately. Failure to do so will result in your (and your partners') death, losing everything you brought in.
Every firearms had something to offer; each gun had its own strengths and weaknesses, so there was no such thing as "trash weapon" nor "superb weapon," meaning that you would always have a chance to topple over enemies, if you know how to play your gun right.
The world and environment is something that no other game would be able to pull off, its occult-esque darkness surrounding the world, which can be found both in-game in the lore book, i.e. the Book of Weapons and the Book of Monsters. The events pre-1896 were on track with its lore and brought interesting seasonal addition into the game in the form of short stories (and some cool narrations along with them).

But right now, after Hunt's 1896 reboot, everything matters no more. They completely removed all the books from the game, so we can't even have a look of the game's lores anytime you want (Crytek did announced that the books will be available on Hunt website, but why ripping them away from the game in the first place?).
Gunfight-wise, they've started to add more and more broken weapons and traits which makes any strategic aspects completely useless. They are now encouraging more fast-paced fights by implementing absurd equipment and buffing up more spammy weapons. They made every gun have all same custom ammo, made every shotgun buffed, made more expensive weapons powerful, and de-penalized being downed with Revive Bolt and Restoration Shot. The worst weapon so far is the "Shredder," a crossbow-ish weapon that shoots sawblades semi-auto that ricochet off the walls and home on enemies in proximity. That's the most absurd mechanics I've ever seen in any other shooter games (other than CoD), and it doesn't even fit into the game's original gunplay system in any way. They completely lost touch on what to do with equipment and are only focusing on attracting [i]major audience[/i] by steering away Hunt's core gameplay.

What dove a final nail in the coffin is the recent event, Post Malone's Murder Circus. Before this event, at least themes of each event were always on par with Hunt's originality. But the Murder Circus is all for Post Malone, a real-life celebrity (evident as shown in its title). Almost all weapon skin has a "PM" initials engraved, and there are two Post Malone Hunter skins in the battle pass. If I ever wanted to see a famous musician or actor, I'd go play CoD or Fortnite. I liked Hunt for its own unique atmosphere, not for having a real-life celebrity.

I don't know what to think of Hunt: Showdown anymore. This isn't [i]the[/i] Hunt I used to know. Once a dark, tense and slow-paced game, with an actually fine-balanced equipment, has become nothing but a so-called "Western" run-and-gun trigger-happy shooter. I may come back when my Hunt partners group up for a couple of matches, but I'm not going to actively play this game onwards.

Talk about an atmospheric gameplay experience, Hunt Showdown is a gorgeous horror shooter stealth game with the sole intent of having the players immersed in a chilling western environment where each single match could be the last.

Right off the bat, this is not a game that belongs in the oversaturated Battle Royale market. No. Hunt Showdown is a very unique arena shooter that involves both PvE and PvP. In fact, the remarkable aesthetic and art style are breathtakingly amazing. Combined with the absolutely fantastic sound design, the world presented is awe-inspiring and scary beyond imagination.

With only 1 opened world map, 2 bosses and only a handful of enemies, there just doesn't seem to be a lot of variety at the moment. The gunplay, on the other hand, is marvelous! Though the combat is slow paced, the shooting is one of the best aspects of the game, making you really concentrate your fire when needed.

All the many details implemented, such as the different weather style, unnerving sounds (damn twig snaps), and even the user interface, make it a special kind of horror. All throughout the match there is never a death count or actual indication of what exactly is going down. You might hear gunshots in the distance thinking people are duke it out, but you won't know the outcome. That makes for really good tension.

It feels to me like Hunt Showdown could end up being a niche title, not a bad thing, because even though the progression system is very rewarding, the perma death element ( meaning that once the hunter you've recruited gets killed off, they stay dead) might not be everyone's cup of tea.

Honestly, Crytek have a lot to improve here, especially when it comes to the performance, but it has the potential of being a very solid multiplayer game. Give it a try!

Steam keeps on bothering me to write a review for this game so here's one , i guess.

You might have heard this ' there's nothing like it on the market ' description of Hunt : Showdown and frankly i must admit that it is mostly spot on. This game is pretty unique and intriguing mix of PVE and PVP within setting which i frankly doubt i ever really saw used in a video game before. We are talking about end of 19th century Louisiana  mixed with paranormal horror activity.

If you would take a super brief look at Hunt's gameplay loop one could mistakenly assume that it is a battle royal game and while there are few similarities between the two, Hunt has a really original and unique gameplay loop i have never seen done before in a video game.

Core idea here is that you enter a map , which is 1km x 1km square , either alone , in a duo or a trio of hunters and your main goal is to look for clues to locate a boss , kill him , banish him and extract with a bounty. Sounds simple enough , right? But that is there fun actually behinds. Besides having to contend with PVE part of the game , that is various kind of AI controlled zombies ( for the lack of better word ) , number of sound traps like injured animals ,crows ,caged chickens and dogs ( of whom all make loud noises then disturbed in turn giving out your location and even direction you are moving in ) , you are also not alone in a pursuit of that bounty. That is there PVP part of game kicks in .

Even  though this is  PVPVE game , PVE is here only to slow down you rather than being a real threat. Real threat comes from other players who also have same goal as you. Real 'meat' of this game is PVP and while you can choose and avoid PVP all together , you will not have much fun while doing so. Bosses , again , are mostly there to funnel players into the same area to initiate PVP fights.

PVP is rough and tough in Hunt. From what i understand earlier in it's life it was even more hardcore , but even at it's current state this game is not for faint hearted folks. Kill times are low , weapons are mostly single shots so each shot counts ( fitting the settings and time period ) and while on a surface this could look like a simple point and shoot situation there are dozens upon dozens of systems and things to consider in each firefight so you will need tens and in some cases hundreds of hours to really start to feel what are you doing. 

 I wont lie to you , for first 20 or 30 hours i was pretty much cowering behind stuff in each firefights in essence being a glorified decoy for enemy players while my team mate hopefully was doing something less useless.  Hunt can be really stressful with steep learning curve, perma death ( losing your hunter with all his/her equipment you spent so much money on ) and never knowing who has your in their scopes while crossing open fields but it also can be so very rewarding when you survive a final server wide gunfight on your last bullet and out of healing items. Even 140 hours in some of the firefights leaves me with my heart pounding which is a rare occasion after playing video games and FPS game for more than 25 years now.

There are of course bunch of technical issues, questionable decisions from the dev team and other negatives associated with any competitive online game so be aware of that before you decide to enter Bayou .

After small investment of 2200 hours in this journey, Time of Review has come. Let's dive in the mechanically best shooter on the market, developed by company that does not want to respect player time or money. 

There are few truly great aspects but they are being overshadowed quickly by obnoxious business practices and devs distancing from playerbase and ignoring feedback.

Best of all mechanics - the audio. You can learn to distinguish any weapon and distance it was shot at by sound cues alone. Game knowledge of weapon ammo pools and approximate fire rates helps to crawl out alive from firefights. You can also listen for victims inside buildings and pinpoint their location based even on what they are walking on to surprise some louder fella through walls to secure a kill or at least give a serious scare. 
Having a decent audio gear makes traversing this world a real treat. 

Huge recommendation for their own in-house band - Port Sulphur Band. They are making enjoyable soundtracks that are making their way into daily music playlists of mine.

Close behind audio chases the gunplay. Game is set in late 19th century, all of the guns are satisfying to play, majority of weapons are semi-auto and single shot, with impactful reloads that take time and are audible. All of weapons made as historically accurate as possible without affecting viability in game with few deviations. Instant head-shot kill mechanic makes weapon balance mostly a non-issue personally. 

Maps are superbly designed, they are spacious, but not feeling desolate. Each map consists of 16 compounds that are diverse and all of them have meticulously crafted multiple approaches for more unpredictable gameplay loop.

Trait art style - No gameplay impact, just beauty, have to give a shout-out. Artist should be proud.

Now that positive aspects have been covered, time to cover the marketing and lovely customer support/feedback:

This atrocity can not be called a game anymore, it is just a monetisation incarnate. If You hear about earning in-game currency (Blood Bonds) by just playing or developers caring about the game, that reflects a bygone era. 
Now monetisation rapidly worsening and is comparable to mobile game industry, while by itself it would not affect gameplay - there is our first real issue - most updates focus on new skins rather than fixing bugs and exploits that are game-breaking and are still accessible. Fixing bugs unfortunately for Crytek can not be sold for 10 bucks a month.
During a month we are getting approximately 5 skins to be purchasable in-game with Blood Bonds(BB) and 1-2 10 EUR DLCs. Altogether some 40+ EUR a month worth of skins. With in game skins being so badly priced the 10 EUR DLC seems like a good deal. It still is not, frankly, especially when that money does not show any effect by fixing the game.

To make it worse - almost all means of earning in game currency by playing are gone. The only reliable remaining system "Challenges" is getting increasingly more grindy despite constant player feedback. 
Considering that people bought this game with premise of earning the BBs by playing, this is blatant scam and possibly only reason that we have this Challenge reward system is to avoid legal trouble of fraud.
Before summer 2023 You gained BBs just by playing the game and meeting different milestones during match, rewarding a good performance, now only time You get rewarded is when You enter CVV.
Obtaining a skin this way takes 5 months due to hard cap introduced by their monetisation manager. Or the same cost for a battlepass, that lasts 3 months and is getting intentionally more grindy due to progression being tied to the Challenges.

Crytek also seem to have done some extensive research and come to ground-breaking conclusion - event means player spike, and that is why the base game has been inaccessible for almost a year now.
They are using events as beta to test new features which never get hotfixed and just block base gameplay. Events are being released one after another with 14-30 days in-between. People take break from game for two weeks missing base game due to burn out from event grind just to be greeted by another event after two weeks.

At this point we are observing new way to release a game. Instead of early access hell this game is reverting from full release to beta permanently.

Community has requested separate non-event queue, but that falls on deaf ears - Quite possible is that they can not put 10 Eur mark on separate matchmaking. Yet.
This event spam has also made the gunplay considerably worse and that is the reason why it falls behind soundwork. Previously each gun had few custom ammo types that have different effects (e.g. set target ablaze, bleed, poison). Now most weapons share almost all the types making game knowledge less relevant, not possible to narrow down possible threats.
Game is steering towards one best meta weapon having all the ammos and other weapons losing any importance.
These events also are usually released with balance patches, that are main reason people are usually trying the game again, in hopes of fixed bugs and exploits and people not spamming same weapon (SPOILER ALERT: nothing changes, so we have same player drop off yet again). 

FOMO practices is horror level - timed battlepass, progressively more grindy weekly to earn BBs, event limited skins.
 
Next huge issue is cheaters. And sadly due to marketing this is not going to change.
Soft-cheaters and blatant cheaters both infest this game.
Soft cheating also known as "Ping-abusing". Hits are registered client side, while the idea is nice - not letting people with worse internet to struggle behind - we are running into people abusing this as META. Players are connecting to servers on other side of the world and/or using VPN to increase the ping to gain advantage. This is also practiced by streamers and Crytek partners.
Due to this ping-abusing You may die as far as 10-20 meters from the place You were on Your screen. Even their "Kill View" system shows Your body miles away from the place where the shot was registered.
Blatant cheaters are the ones that use aimbot through walls from other side of map instantly after spawning as the worst case and just wall/aim hackers as the most tame.

And here also comes the lovely customer support and player feedback.

People are giving absolutely positive feedback about previously reduced grind in Challenge system - Grind gets increased and complaints ignored.
People are requesting separate non-event queue to actually enjoy game as they bought it at least once a year - Ignored
People are requesting to limit ping to servers to avoid soft-cheating - Ignored
People are reporting blatant cheaters through CS, as it is only place Crytek allows it - They are still running with same account and cheats without any consequences.

Feedback falls on deaf ears unless it can be sold for money or better look for investors. And Crytek is allowing cheating just to not reduce player numbers by banning. There is no other explanation why cheaters that are reported with video proof are not being banned at all.

Latest event is recycling parts of previous event, possibly due to rushed release to retain players, because player bleed to other releases is unforgivable sin. With all the increasing grind and event spam having another game to play, a job or - god forbid - a family is heretic sin in eyes of Crytek. Only people that play their game exclusively matter. And even those do not matter enough that their feedback would be relevant.

I'll be making this as informative as possible for any potential buyers out there, so please bear with me. This game is regarded as a hardcore, niche shooter that began as a PVE (Player versus Environment) title that was converted to PVP (Player versus Player) with PVE elements as the Battle Royal fad picked up steam. 

*My suggestion at the start is; don't buy it yet, but keep an eye on it.*
    
The ultimate purpose of each match is to locate clues to triangulate a npc boss placed randomly around the map, kill it, banish it to hell, then grab a bounty token as proof of the kill and finally extract to three randomly generated locations on the outskirts of the map. As you attempt to fulfill this task, you'll likely engage some NPC enemies as they've heavily populated the map and have converged on various settlements. Not only that, but you're running the risk of engaging with other players, and then killing them. 
    
The AI enemies exist to redirect players, force them to give away their position by combat, serve as an unconventional warning system to nearby players and lastly to complicate existing shootouts between players. Mind you, they are actually deadly and can easily kill you if you're caught in a pinch. Fortunately for you lot, they're stupid. 

First things first, no weapon in this game operates on a hitscan mechanic but on an actual projectile system. Hitscan mechanics are very popular among shooters, as you only need to place your crosshairs on a target and pull the trigger to deal damage. Hunt's true projectile system requires you to know the speed of your ammunition type and to lead your shots appropriately to fight effectively. Hunt places an incredible amount of emphasis on sound, as players make noises no AI can replicate and are the only things capable of triggering sound traps. It could be argued that you'll hear your opponents before you see them, so ambushes are highly likely. Your goal is to get the bounty, but killing players often takes precedent.

Regarding soundtraps, they're everywhere. Gatherings of crows and ducks which get spooked if a player gets too close, to dying horses and caged animals which break out into a frenzy should you approach. Shards of glass scattered on the ground, hanging kitchenware, bottles, horseshoes and chains. The cries of the AI enemies if they detect a player. The sounds of players grunting as they fight the AI. Simply moving around makes noise depending on the surface upon which you travel: dry dirt, mud, wooden planks, fallen branches, metal roofs and water. Gunshots will ring out from incredible distances, with certain guns being more noticeable.

There are five projectile speeds in the game, technically six. Starting from slowest to fastest, we have: Thrown items, Crossbow bolts, Compact, Shotshells, Medium and Long. It could be argued that thrown items don't count, but I've placed them here for informative purposes.  Learning the relative speeds of your ammuntion type and the weapons that utilize them is the foundation for combat. Generally speaking, you'll start the game with weapons using shotgun shells and compact ammo. Crossbow bolts and medium ammo using weapons are unlocked rather mid to late bloodline, whereas long ammo weapons are mostly late bloodline options.

The Bloodline is one of two leveling mechanics Hunt features. It is your direct account level, and governs the unlocking of weapons, traits, cash prizes and hunter tiers. Hunter tiers used to provide substantial benefits, a Tier 3 hunter would have 150 health compared to a Tier 1 possessing 100. This was removed a while ago, so now higher Tier hunters only bring cosmetic changes and potentially better equipment and traits when you hire them. The second leveling mechanic is the hunters themselves. If you successfully extract from a mission alive, your hunter is rewarded experience based on what you did in the mission and levels up. Leveling your hunter gives you more perk points, which are used to purchase traits for your hunter. Your bloodline simply unlocks the trait, but you must level your hunter and then purchase the trait. This is locked to the hunter himself, and if he dies they're gone forever. You'll need to level another hunter in order to purchase the trait again, or get lucky in the recruitment phase and hire a hunter already featuring the trait. This mechanic empowers those who survive, making them more resilient to the environment or more deadly outright with the proper traits.

-With the implementation of the quickplay mode, players have the opportunity to play at no risk in an actual battle royal. You rush to find 4 items of interest, and then if you're the first to get 4 your goal is to survive. The longer you're alive the more money you'll walk away with, even if you die. If someone beats you to the punch, you'll need to kill them and take the objective for yourself. This mode allows low leveled players to potentially get and use endgame weapons and traits. However, you can take these weapons into the original mode only if you win the quickplay mission. This means that skilled players can easily get strong loadouts for free, with the added benefit of the contraband status on your equipment. With quickplay, money is no consequence, since playing the mode exclusively results in free money and bloodline experience; with the added benefit of a No Risk High Reward loadout should you win.

 I'll wrap things up here with what I feel is the outright cons. 
-The game is incredibly unforgiving to new players. Combat against players is very different than against AI, therefore trial and error is the name of the early game. Doesn't help that low rank gear and equipment is laughable in comparison to everything else.
-An actual practice range isn't in the game, it's on the roadmap for the future but that means you're on your own. Basically it means that you'll learn to swim by jumping off a boat.  
-A while back compact ammunition provided low rank players with the potential to kill higher ranked players with a headshot at long range. High rank players complained to the point where the devs nerfed the ammo type to prevent long range sniping, meaning that high rank hunters can one tap you from a distance in which you'll need to hit them twice. This was regarded as a nerf to skill, by some players.
-The community is rather hostile to new people on the steam discussion forums. This is a niche, hardcore shooting game. Any suggestions to make things easier for newer players or to make the game more appealing to a wider audience usually gets shot down quickly. 
-Unoptimized game across many different rigs.
-Suffers from low player count, you're often put into empty games or repeatedly matched with the same/higher ranked players.
-Quickplay provides a zero risk way to quickly get money and Bloodline ranks, compared to the main Bounty Hunt mode.
-Matchmaking is based on two key points, Hunter Kills/Deaths and Bounties extracted. If you play a bunch of empty games and extract several bounties you'll likely be matched with players with large amounts of kills. Bounties being extracted equals a material advantage.
-Existing playerbase is divided by 7 regions, then 2 game modes, and lastly 3 different bounties on the base game mode, Bounty Hunt.
-Currently there isn't much of a temptation to prestige in this game outside of personal challenge and promises of unspecified future rewards. The result is players reaching rank 100 and just sitting there forever, at rank 100 you gain a constant cash flow and retain access to all items. 
-There's rumbling in the distance in regards to the Dev's stability; they're apparently shifting from adding new content to optimization for several months out. 

In conclusion I stress the following: Don't buy it yet, but keep an eye on it.

EDIT: They're bringing in premium currency and microtransactions. It looks like it'll be cosmetic for now, but we all know how slippery a slope that is huh?

[b]Crytek[/b]

It's been a while since Ryse: Son of Rome, the last AAA Crytek-developed game I played. I am also familiar with their Crysis franchise. I was glad to read the news on a western-themed FPS software. I found it interesting that instead of the story this game would be focusing on multiplayer. It's been 3 years since Hunt Showdown was released (originally under the early access concept) and new content has been added ever since. 

[b]Game mechanics - the 4 stages[/b]

With a friend or 2 (or alone if we're brave enough) our job is to look for clues in a huge map. A special visibility mode helps with the search. The aim here is to find information on a boss (or 2 bosses) that are considered the bounties during our match. Once the boss is found we, naturally, have to eliminate it. These are monsters - terrifying, otherwordly creatures - that hide inside a large building. As the 2nd stage is done we begin banishing the vanquished creature. Consider it an automatically applied spell that takes some time and we have to remain in position. After that we can pick up our well-deserved bounty and go to one of the extraction points that are randomly chosen.

Interesting, right? This is the PvE part of the game but it is PvP as other hunters also look for the same bounty. It is my understanding that matches support up to 12 players. It can be very annoying when you finally eliminate the boss and then you're suddenly shot down. Or during extraction (there is a timer of 30 seconds here) you are killed before taking home your well-deserved reward.

[b]Sergio Leone in the supernatural[/b]

The setting may be the late 1800s but not your usual one. The story takes place in Louisiana so expect a lot of swamps with trees and - most importantly - otherwordly creatures. There are grunts (living dead but often with melee weapons), armored grunts, hell hounds, zombies on fire (immolators), undead releasing swarms of insects at you from a distance (hives) and even the devil (?) is trying to get you in the water if you are not careful. As if all had come from a Lucio Fulci classic.

[b]Headset recommended[/b]

The sound design is superb in this game be it your steps or the noises an enemy makes. You need to be careful when moving around - stepping on broken glasses just after entering a building or bumping your head into a bunch of hanging horseshoes can all be giveaways. I have played every single match with my headset on and it was worth it. Interestingly, ingame voice chat when used can also be heard if other players are close. People use Discord or Steam's built-in version instead.

[b]Hunters[/b]

Consider them your heroes. You have some already available but more can be recruited for money. They level up individually as you complete matches but your profile also has ranks. Higher ranks unlock more traits (abilities) that you can assign to your hunters as well as new weapons. Remember, this is the Wild West (or South...) so expect to reload after every single shot. This is not running and gunning like in a Call of Duty game. A dinamite takes much longer to explode than a grenade. 

Oh, dinamites. There are a lot of throwables, traps, even several choices for melee weapons. The DLCs here mean purely cosmetic items (better skins for the afore-mentioned). Legendary heroes are a bit different - beside the cosmetic aspect (they look unique) and the short bio they come with these hunters have randomly assigned traits. They can come handy at the beginning but they will never have weapons on them.

[b]Matchmaking and other issues[/b]

I'm based in Europe but I picked US East Coast as the secondary location for matches. Often one is found in the second group only. In general, finding matches takes long. If there is just one boss players hardly advance to find clues but instead camp out and wait for you. 

The game resurrects your hunters until you reach rank 11. It warns you that after that your hunters will perish forever. The legendary ones (DLC) you can always buy again but every time they start out as level 1. So, you lose all traits and all weapons. Why from rank 11? If you complete a match and die you only get half the XP. Two groups of people will never level up at the same speed following the same number of matches. 

When you get shot you see your enemy was a level 1 hunter, for instance. But before moving onto spectating you can check the other players' profiles. They may be level 1 but the statistical data shown to you is surprising (and disappointing): dozens or even hundreds of bosses or duo groups eliminated already and dozens of hunters retired (advisable once your hunter has reached the max level). 

As you can see from the above the game is extremely unforgiving. Beginners (or noobs in the vocabulary of some) are punished if mistakes are made. I always spectate and check the other players - I usually see players with ranks between 60 and 100. No newcomers? It's been 3 years and a 3rd map is about to be released and really we have a small playerbase consisting of veterans mostly? You can pick the "skill-based" option before starting matchmaking but if the other player has played hundreds of hours already he is better with the same level 1 hunter. Not to mention the kind of gear available for them already. The pop-up message can say we are equally based but, in fact, this is not true, at all.

[b]Summary[/b]

Apart from the above the game is gorgeous. The atmosphere is unique and it makes absolute no sense playing it without a headset on. It is unfortunate that matchmaking has issues, that the game is harsh to newcomers and that beside the usual bountyhunting there is only one other game mode available which puts emphasis on solo play. With the track record of some great story-based games I wish Crytek added a single player mode. 

I recommend the game due to its unique atmosphere and slow-paced gameplay style but you have to remember I'm (still) at the very beginning while I have so far invested 20 hours. This is not a "easy to learn, hard to master" type of game if that is what you're looking for. The score in particular is great in the main menu!

*edit* I nominated the game for "Labour of Love" this year (2022). Such a shame the constant update messages on Steam are full of troll messages.

Hunt Showdown has been the best experience I've had with a shooter so far.

The game is a pvp & pve stealth game, but it can also be played more fast pace, though the game is designed to be played slower and with a more careful approach, since every small decision or mistake can lead to you being discovered or possibly killed.

PROS:

+The gunplay is a lot of fun and makes perfect sense for this type of game.
The guns feel like they got weight to them, kind of clunky but true to the era.
The clunkiness of the weapons also impacts your playstyle and when you decide to shoot, because every shot counts, due to the scarcity of ammo and other ressources and because you might be discovered by other players in your area.

+The game design and setting is beautiful, dark and unique.
This western setting with monsters and grim lore makes for a perfect pvp survival shooter experience.
The map design is smart and beautiful. 
Every location looks different and has many obstacles and covers where you can hide behind during gunfights. Due to this no gunfight feels the same.

+The sounddesign is unlike any other multiplayer shooter game's.
You can perfectly estimate distances and directions of shots or footsteps of other players.
Every enemy-type makes different sounds when being aggroed, attacked or killed, so if you alert an enemy, other players in the area will surely know.

+The Mobs actually pose a threat.
Mobs are usually oneshot-kills, except for the bosses, but if you are being attacked by other players in addition to the mobs, you are almost sure to killed. 

+The perk system is balanced.
You can have a maxed out hunter and still be killed by level one hunters who have no perks.
The perks are great and make certain things easier for the build you're going for, but they don't make you overpowered.

+Recruiting and equiping hunters with weapons and items makes for a fun survival experience.
Once your hunter dies on a mission you lose every progress you made with him, which makes the decisions you make feel like they have an impact, and usually you don't just rush enemies, because unlike other shooters you don't respawn instantly after being killed. You have to recruit and equip a new hunter before being able to go on another mission.

CONS:

-Sometimes mobs just spawn right in front of you, or further away.
This takes you out of the experience or could potentially even spook you.

-Sometimes the outline of objects don't work.
For example, sometimes you will be shooting between two treebranches and the bullet will impact in the air between the two branches because the outline is sometimes not precise, which can be very frustrating when you're engaged in a firefight.

-It's hard to recommend the game to friends because the learning curve is incredibly long.
I've played the game for 300h  and i still feel like i'm making rookie mistakes.
Which is both challenging and annoying at times.

CONCLUSION:

I can really recommend this game to anyone who likes survival shooters and stealth oriented games.
The game is very immersive and dark which no game has pulled off as well as Hunt Showdown, especially since it's a multiplayer game.
For anyone looking for a challenging pvp & pve game, this is your game.

With the realise of 1.0 the Devs decided to completely change many aspects of the game. One of the initial biggest attractions for many people to Hunt was the fact that the game had a dark, gritty look which was also echoed in the tough, unforgiving nature of the game. It was a slow, tactical game which could burst into action at any moment, whether it be PvP action or you just accidentally wandered in to the middle of a pack of Hellhounds and the resulting noise attracted everything in the vicinity. Unfortunately 1.0 changes a lot of these 

The graphics are nowhere near as clear or consistent as they were at launch, they have upped the lighting to the point where the once pitch black night is not dark at all. They have reduced the LOD so much that texture pop-ins happen all the time, this is really off putting in a stealth game when you are looking for enemies in the distance in trees/bushes.

Up until 1.0 aiming in Hunt was a two step process, One button to bring your gun up into hipfire stance then another button press to bring you into ADS stance. This, along with some pretty severe weapon sway meant that gunfights in Hunt used to require a great deal of skill. Even people with incredible aim couldn't just one tap everyone from anywhere. It meant fights on average lasted longer than other FPS games and this required players to be more than just a 'Good Shot' in engagements, flanking, retreating and re-engaging, using decoys or even triggering AI to help you win fights all happened frequently. However the introduction of 'Gunslinger' mode allows players to bypass the two stage aiming system, with Gunslinger the player is always in hipfire stance, meaning they have an advantage on anyone not using Gunslinger as they only have to press one button to shoot instead of two, and although the Devs claim there is a disadvantage to using Gunslinger I have yet to see where any disadvantage lies. The removal of the weapon sway has meant that anyone with halfway decent aim can get headshots quite easily, both of these changes have reduced the skill ceiling whilst also reducing the average length of gunfights which in turn has seen a reduction in the need to flank etc. This has imo made the game a little boring. If I wanted insanely accurate guns and fast gunfights I wouldn't be playing a game like Hunt as there are so many other games that allow me to play that way easier and with more enjoyment and variance.  

They also decided to add a 3d pinging system, it feels so out of place in the game it's ridiculous. I realise they wanted a way for random teams to communicate without using in game VOIP but instead of having the mark only appear on the compass they make it 3d, reducing a huge skill in the game which was being able to quickly and accurately describe the location of an enemy.

As far as I'm concerned the Devs have spent over a year and a half making a game that caters to the audience that initially bought the game and supported it an audience that loved the slow paced, stealth and tactical heavy requirements, only for them to turn around and slap those supporters in the face by springing a dumbed down, easier to play and more accessible to the average player version of the game just before full launch. It reeks of a lack of confidence in the original concept and gameplay and stinks of a company who are struggling financially screwing over those that where there when needed in order to chase that mainstream cash. 

I've been eagerly awaiting the full release of this game for nearly 2 years and I couldn't be more disappointed in the outcome.

Edit to add: I didn't realise that 1.0 increased the price to £36 for the little content in this game (two maps, 3 Bosses) it really isn't worth it with that price point.

One of my favorite games I've ever played. The setting and aesthetic is peak, the sound design is solid, and the gunplay generally feels good. Certainly one of the most fun games in the extraction shooter genre.

It's also a $40 game, the devs put out a new $10-15 cosmetic dlc every month, routinely rotate in events that feature a paid battle pass, and has a premium currency skin shop in-game. I didn't used to mind this, because this game also featured one of the better premium currency systems in any game I had played. Kill a few players? You get some blood bonds (the premium currency in this game) Extract with a bounty token? You get some blood bonds. Complete your weekly challenges? You get some blood bonds. If you were a decent player and played a good amount every week when the shop rotated you could get one or sometimes more of the skins that got discounted every week without ever paying in a cent. If you never spent beyond a certain threshold you could earn the battle pass for free every event. It was great. And then update 1.13 happened.

With update 1.13, Crytek made some very good changes to mechanics that used blood bonds in the past that never should have. However, they also completely removed blood bond rewards from accolades, as well as the 25bb for extracting a bounty 5 days in a row. In return, they buffed the reward for completing your weekly challenges from 25 to 50bb. With this, all but one method of earning blood bonds was removed, which drastically shrunk blood bond income. Before, a theoretical "perfect" match would earn you 15bb from accolades. Now, no matter how you did in a match, no bb for you. Crytek got greedy. The most bb you can earn in one week is now 50. No more earning a new skin every week if you play a lot and are decent at the game, instead, more getting shoehorned into doing challenges and playing in ways you maybe don't want to. You want the paid battlepass to get the rewards from it? Assume you start from zero you have to complete all of your weekly challenges every week for 20 weeks to earn it. There are 52 weeks in a year and typically 2 events per year, spaced evenly. That leaves you with 12 weeks to earn blood bonds you get to use on skins you want instead of the battlepass if you want all the battlepass rewards without spending money.

Didn't think I'd ever write a negative review for Hunt, but here we are.

I'd like to preface this by saying that this is from the perspective of a long-time, high-MMR player. I started playing seriously in late 2020, but I had played during early access in 2019 as well for anyone who remembers that. I've been here for the highs and lows, and I think after years of dealing with Crytek making the same mistakes over and over I'm just tired. With every "event" (Which is just a battle-pass season) they introduce more and more clearly broken weapons or traits that aren't just occasionally "broken" in the balance sense (I'll get to that later) but broken on a technical level. 

Peacemaker (Desolation's Wake) was especially egregious. I originally typed out a detailed explanation of why, but scrapped it because I don't want this review to be longer than it's already going to be. Long story short, instead of fixing it during the event, Crytek just put out a statement saying "This is against the rules and bannable" like it already wasn't. There's already a rule stating only organic teaming through VOIP or in-game text chat is allowed, and intentionally teaming before a game was already bannable. If this wasn't bad enough, it took them until the event was half over to even issue this nothing-burger statement. It never got patched. They just said they'd revert XP/Money gained by players who abused it, which didn't fix the root issue of games being ruined for 60 days.

Peacemaker is just my best example, as other traits from previous events had similar - although not as damaging - traits like the Infernal pact which made you immune to (and heal) from fire on top of automatically curing bleed. Paired with bloodless, an antidote shot, and the fact everyone was running it and nothing else for the aforementioned reasons, all status effects in the game were essentially useless, also for 60 days.

Another example on the weapon side is the Spear, and how it invalidated every other tool slot melee weapon for months and months before even being addressed by the devs where it got a nerf that did bring it down a peg but not enough to bring back the choice we once had in that category.

I could go on and on about brain-dead balance decisions over the years (Katana invalidating every other melee weapon, Dolch getting special ammo, some new special ammo being a straight upgrade to default, putting Surefoot in the base game, Lightfoot solo buff messing with the fundamentals, etc) to the point of bloating this review to be pages long, but whoever has the wheel right now genuinely needs to take a step back and listen to people who know how to play the game, or step down and let someone who knows how to play take the wheel. They also contradict themselves so often from patch to patch that it doesn't even seem coherent, the most recent example being nerfing Necromancer because they "Didn't want ranged revives to be spammed" and then adding revive bolts for the hand crossbow a patch or two later, which is ten times worse.

Problem is, they know all of this. They don't care. They balance based on usage metrics and back-end data instead of actually looking at the state of their game. It's the only reason the Uppercut keeps getting bullied; people use it because BIG IRON and they see it's popular and nerf it into the ground. I was in favour of the recent shift to a faster pace at first because I thought the most "Patient" team reliably winning every fight was intensely boring, but recently they've overstepped with Surefoot, revive bolts and really common restoration that removes a lot of the careful decision-making that made combat so interesting. I could go on for hours, I feel like I'm missing so much.

A HUGE issue for me was changing how penetration works and then claiming it was a "bug" that penetration was so good for 5-6 years. It very well could be, but if it took you half a decade to find it, that's on you. You shouldn't lower the skill ceiling just to "fix" something that wasn't a problem in the first place.

I've dealt with this for a long time, and I've always thought they're just finding their footing or they need more time to fix whatever it is they need to fix but after years of neglecting the state of the game and refusing to patch during 60 day blocks, I'm just tired.

They recently, for the first time in years, actually made a balance patch mid-event by slightly nerfing the Shredder, which again, was so busted it shouldn't have even shipped but that's the trend. If they become more hands on in the future I might be more enthusiastic but I have no more patience or hope for change anymore.

The most recent nail in the coffin for me is disregarding the game's atmosphere for IP collabs meant to draw in new players that, in my opinion, feel cheap and desperate. Why does every skin from the current pass need Post Malone's initials stamped on them? The Sparks Pistol has his initials branded on it literally 14 separate times, I wish I was joking. It feels like one of those "Every other popular game is doing it" situations where they feel like they have to as well if they want to break into the mainstream, which I think is misguided given that Hunt will never be mainstream unless they turn it into something else that isn't Hunt. They know this though, and they're working on changing it. Whether or not the game changes for the better or just becomes more generic is up in the air, but from the recent string of changes it's feeling more generic already.

I've already gone on long enough and I haven't mentioned a lot of other problems but it is what it is. The bad is starting to outweigh the good for me but don't get me wrong, I still love the game and want the best for it; I just don't think Crytek knows what to do with the game and it's going to cost them as more competition starts to appear.

If you're a new player, you won't be bothered by a lot of my personal issues with the game. Go ham, have fun. As soon as you climb in MMR (I play in 6) you'll understand, and whether or not you're patient enough to put up with the neglect will be down to you. Good luck.

I've held off writing a review for hunt mainly because I'm lazy and have had no motivation to do such a thing. But now that I get a shiny badge, well, here we go. However rest assured, I will strive to give this game the review it deserves. 

Hunt is a PvEvP game, where a match is limited to 12 players sharing the simple goal of locating a bounty target, banishing it and then extracting with the bounty. Matches can also either be single bounty or dual bounty. The bounty lair is found via clues located within compounds, each clue removes several compounds from the map until only one is left. Hunters must then deal with the boss located within the bounty compound by killing it and then banishing it. After the banish is complete a hunter can loot the bounty and then make their way to 1 of 3 extraction points on the map, whilst defending the bounty they hold from other hunters attempting the claim it as their own.

Now the premise of the game is out of the way let me start off by saying hunt is by far my favourite game. I can get lost in it's world for hours upon end and with the variety of weapons on offer, no two games play out the same. Also unlike other games every weapon in hunt is actually a viable choice, sure hunt has its meta weapons, I'm looking at you long ammo. However given the correct application of any of the individual weapons in game you can come out ontop of any other weapon, no matter how meta it may be. 

That for me is the unique thing about hunt. Due to it's setting in the late 19th century, the guns on offer are mainly limited to slow firing rifles and pistols, along with single and double barrel shotguns. This allows for a skilled environment as the time to kill is quite often how good your aim is. A well placed headshot being the quickest and most effective way of dealing with an enemy hunter, failing that 2 to 3 body shots will often usually do the trick too. That being said hunt is not all about aim, sure it helps and it is most definitely something I need to improve on myself. However you can find success in hunt via other methods as well. Playing smart is probably the most successful way to play hunt, knowing when to push, when to take a shot, when not to take a shot and when to rotate all play a vital part in a hunters success and this will come with time spent in game.

Which brings me nicely onto my next point. Hunt, at least when I first started, was not a welcoming game. You are essentially thrown in at the deep end and left to your own devices. The AI is the first real problem faced by any new player, knowing how to effectively deal with each individual AI type is found out by trial and error. I think everyone, at least once, has knifed an immolator only for it to explode in your face and set you ablaze. But that's how you learn in hunt and rest assured you're not going to forget the lessons taught to you in its brutal world. Even experienced hunters can quickly find themselves dying to AI if they are not paid their due attention. Once you get over the AI then come the enemy hunters themselves, adding a whole other element to the game.

Although I should note I believe attempts have been made to make the game more welcoming over the recent updates, but given the nature of the game I believe it can only be made so welcoming. The once piece of advice I would give new players is to hang in there, because once you get past the steep learning curve, it becomes on of the most rewarding games out there.

I would say for the first 100-200 hours you will be more focused on the PVE aspect of hunt then after this the focus shifts to the PVP aspect. At least in my opinion, I am at the stage where I would much rather have a good gunfight in a match rather than having a match where my team kills and banishes the boss then simply extracts without any PVP conflict. As I know how to deal with the AI, that is not to say it cannot present a problem, because they sure can. But I am at the stage where my learning and progression within the game comes from the PVP encounters. 

Moving onto the community, I would say the hunt community is a welcoming one. I mainly play trios with randoms and 90% of the time encounter friendly, like minded hunters. There are the occasional 'bad eggs' out there, but that is to be expected within any online gaming community in this day in age unfortunately. For example during 1000+ hours I have been team killed once and have witnessed about 2 or 3 team killings from and on my random trio partners. Although it should be noted some hunters will dodge lobbies based upon your loadouts or stats, but this is simply remedied by finding a new trio, which for myself, does not take more than a couple off attempts.  A quick disclaimer I play at 5 star MMR, on occasions dipping to 4. I have also played against and with 6 star MMR players, but never reaching it myself. Thus the above is purely my experience of the hunt community, I cannot speak as to how welcoming the game is for newer players, however any new players I personally come across I am more than happy to give them a few pointers and make them feel welcomed within the community.

If I take my rose tinted glasses off for a few moments then yes there are a few issues with the game. The servers can sometimes play up, with extreme lag. Desync is also an issue, especially when jumping through and over terrain and in some cases can result in the death of a hunter. On rare occasions the compounds will not load or they can take a while to load, resulting in a player seeing nothing where there should be buildings and objects. 

The above issues are what I have experienced first hand, there may be more issues which have been experience by the community. That being said the number of times I have experienced any of the above issues has been minimal, but should be highlighted nonetheless. 

Overall can I recommend hunt showdown? Absolutely. 
The game is unique in it's setting and atmosphere, with one of the best, if not the best, soundtracks out there. It is heavily supported by a dev team that care about the game from a players perspective, with regular updates and regular support for the game. It's a niche game, truly there is nothing else out there like hunt.

This is, simply put, my favourite game.

There's nothing quite like Hunt out there.
It's a difficult, challenging PvPvE game. You play as a bounty hunter tasked with killing a high value target in an area infested with some sort of dark magic. The only problem is, you're not the only hunter out there.

You collect clues to locate the target, you kill the target, you banish the target.... then you have to escape the map with tokens proving it's you who killed it.
Maps can hold 12 players, which means there will be 10 more people who are intent on stopping you leaving with that bounty. And almost everything you do can be heard by everyone else on the map, meaning you have to move as quickly as you can, whilst going as quietly as necessary.

The gameplay loop is incredibly satisfying, with the right balance of risk and reward. Most things you do in a match earn you an amount of cash to take to the next lobby, where you can then either save for a rainy day, or buy higher tier equipment for your next loadout. But, anything you die with is lost to the bayou - hence the risk. If your hunter survives, they get experience and you can use that to buy some traits that make them marginally better for the next run out.

This system sounds like a "win more" system, where success leads to a higher probability of success on the next run, and so it seems inevitable that the good get better equipment to be even more effective - so how can a new player break in?
The answer is quite simple; all equipment has a situation where it's the best choice. The starting rifle has a larger magazine than most other guns in the game and shoots more quickly, so favours closer quarters fighting. The starting shotgun has the longest one-hit-kill range of all the shotguns. Ultimately, playing to your loadout's strengths and being better than your opponent has a FAR higher contribution to your success than the exact equipment everyone loaded in with.

The barrier to a new player is therefore not an insurmountable equipment difference, it's learning the game. There are (currently) three VERY full maps, each of which is absolutely crammed with minutiae. It's about knowing how to move around compounds without triggering sound traps quickly. It's about knowing which directions you're actually vulnerable from. It's about knowing which sort of gun can shoot through that wooden wall you know they're crouched behind. It's about knowing that when the shot sounds like THAT, that means it's this specific gun and how far away they are. The burden of knowledge you have to accumulate to become proficient is very high.

It's this burden of knowledge which is the thing you, as a potential buyer, have to consider.
Are you prepared to get shot from places you don't understand for 20 hours? Are you prepared to be surprised by what their equipment did? You will likely die a lot before you get good.

But when you DO become proficient, there is nothing like this game.
Nothing replicates the thrill of you and a partner (or two) methodically outmanoeuvring another team and taking them down.

Another (major) point in the "pro" column is the developer team. They are extremely active with the community, and listen to and implement suggestions from the community very proactively. They are continually improving the game and adding loads of content. I have bought a lot of the (cosmetic) DLC, purely to support the team, as I have gotten way more out of the game than the price I paid to get in.

Despite every other shooter I try, I keep coming back to Hunt. As long as there are other hunters to go up against, I think I might never stop.

I think after ~1000hrs of play I should write a few words about this game. 

I'm over 40 and honestly I never thought I'd be playing an FPS game with a competitive element in it ever again. I thought I don't have the patience for this and wouldn't get any fun out of being pushed around by people who are way better at clicking heads than me. I was both right and wrong on this...

[h1]Strategic gameplay[/h1]
The most surprising thing for me was that this game is as much about strategy as it is about shooting. I'd even go so far as to say that movement, knowing when to be stealthy, when to be fast, where to go to gain an environment advantage and when to take fights and when to run win you more encounters than straight up shooting. 

This is in part because the game is mostly played at close to mid range and sound plays a crucial role in decision making. Everything you do makes noise, running vs walking vs crounching make different amount of noise, the kind of terrain you're going over also makes different sounds - metal, wood, concrete, soil etc. Opening doors, climbing ladders, reloading your gun, using tools etc. On top of that the environment is littered with sound traps and ai that also makes noise when you engage with it: dying animals makin noise or birds taking off when you go near them, ai enemies making noises. And of course shooting your guns or making melee attacks - everything can be heard by other players depending on how close they are to you. 

This means people can know where you are without even seeing you and smarter players will use this to their advantage, either by making an ambush for your loud ass or simply using that information in combat to attack you with an advantage.

There are ways to deal with sound traps without triggering them (crouch-walking makes minimal sound for example), and weapons that make little to no noise, but they are usially short range and or have other disadvantages (like drop-off for crossbow bolts etc), there are even decoys and fake dynamite sticks to throw people off your trail. 

Did I mention you can place ground traps other people (including yourself - don't ask me how I know) can walk into and take damage?

[h1]Steep learning curve[/h1]
All of the above makes Hunt a vey hard game to get into. With 3 maps spanning over a dozen locations each it's a lot to take in for a new player. To play this game effectively you litterally need to learn these so well that you can instictively navigate them during intense battles. You need to know where the entrances are, where the soundtraps are, where the angles are etc. Learning to spot tools (like medkits) in the environments etc.

The other half is learning how to use that information and making smart plays instead of peeking out of the same window twice to catch a bullet between your eybrows. Also about developing proper habits to take in your surroindings and maybe not make more noise than necessary, or even simply knowing what information you may be giving your opponnent by moving.

It really helps to have friends with enough patience (which I'm lucky to have, thanks guys <3) to help you along and teach the important lessons about the game. Considering a single game usually lasting around 30 minutes, it is going to take a long time before you get comfortable enough to know what's what. 

Hell, you'll be getting killed from angles you didn't know about hundreds of hours in (I'm still finding out about some of the less often used ones!)

[h1]You can revive your teammates[/h1]
Which is such a cool mechanic because if you die, you are not necessarily relegated to spectator mode for the rest of the match. Your teammates can pick you up to 4 times, tho you will have less max hp each time. They either need to get on top of your body or have a skill that allows them to do that from a short distance. There is of course counterplay to that in the form of leaving traps on the the dead players corpse or burning it down (then you can only be picked up by teammates who have the bounty token and they have to sacrifice their own max hp). Players can also put out the flame.

This adds a cool dynamic to team fights and also a way to pressure your opponent.

[h1]Mature, serious themes[/h1]
This is another thing that makes Hunt great is the overall mature theme of the game. There aren't any colorful or joke skins,  emotes to meme on your oponent etc. Everything in the game is thematically appropriate to its setting and that really sets a great mature tone for the game, gives it that gritty realism (even tho you're mowing down lovecraftian enemies)

[h1]Balanced[/h1]
It's also worth mentioning that the devs keep the game pretty well balanced. While there are 'meta' loudouts and a few guns that are pretty much better than anything else there is a lot of room to play whatever you want. Disregarding a few weapons most stuff is actually playable and has enough identity that might make it more preferable for you. A headshot from any weapon can kill. 

There are also some loadouts that offer different playstyle that can take people off-guard. Things that are a bit more spicy than simply shooting bullets at people. Bow and crossbows are a thing and have some very unique ammo types for a more stealthy type of play, there are melee weapons and a melee harpoon type weapon. 

What I'm trying to say that taking 'better' weapons doesn't mean you have an advantage over other players.

[h1]Events![/h1]
There are often long-lasting events that make changes to the gameplay, spicing it up by having new objectives, new abilities for your hunters or even new map weather effects. These usually alter the gameplay in a significant enough way that makes it interesting and new and have only been getting better and better since I started playing. This is a huge part of why I can't get enough of the game even after this many hours.

[h1]Nitpicks[/h1]
There are a few nitpicks I should mention:

1) There can be some voodoo required to make the game behave. I've personally had the game stutter occasionally during fights (even with good ~120 fps) which went away after tuning some gfx settings. A friend had the game randomly crash which turned out to be a hardware issue. It can be tricky to figure out since the game has some quirks and there aren't really any tried solutions in the community forums. 
2) There are also some minor weird bugs happening now and again, usually not affecting gameplay too much, but not always. Luckily the more annoying ones happen very rarely.
3) The game is not patched often, and the devs seem to have a policy of waiting for an event to end before acting. This can be irritating when there's an agreement in the community that there is a balance problem, which can (and has) lead to times where some trait or ammo type or playstyle is noticably better than others, or has little counterplay other than straight up beating them in a fight. This tends to make the game a bit stale for a while since majority of players will be playing the same thing until it is changed or the event ends. 
4) On the patch thing, the devs tend to come down with the nerf-hammer hard at times, addressing things that the community complains about to a degree that they become pretty much unplayable. 

None of these make the game any less fun for me, but it's something that I hope gets better in future :)
